newsitem.title: USA: NABE sees U.S. growth slowing in rest of 1997.
newsitem.headline: NABE sees U.S. growth slowing in rest of 1997.

text.p: The U.S. economy will cool off from the red-hot pace of growth in the first quarter and sustain modest growth with low inflation through 1998, a 37-member panel of the National Association of Business Economists (NABE) said on Tuesday.

The business group boosted its estimate for 1997 gross domestic product (GDP) growth to 3.4 percent from 2.6 percent in its February outlook, adjusting for the surprising 5.6 percent GDP growth in the first quarter. The February NABE survey showed a first-quarter forecast of just 2.0 percent.

"These increases reflected the surge in real output in the first quarter, which was much stronger than the group had expected," the group's report stated, though it left its 1998 GDP forecast at 2.0 percent.
The current second quarter of 1997 should see GDP rise by 2.2 percent, the group said.
The consumer price index will rise 2.8 percent in 1997 and 1998, the group said, slightly lower forecasts than the 1997 2.9 percent and 1998 3.0 percent predictions in the February survey.
While 60 percent of survey participants said they would prefer steady monetary policy over the next six months, 84 percent said they expect the Federal Reserve to raise short-term interest rates.
But the median forecast was for the Fed to tighten by only 25-50 basis points.
The group cited a Congressional Budget Office estimate that the U.S. economy can grow no faster than 2.1 percent without triggering higher inflation in the long run.
Two-thirds of the panelists said they saw no recession until 1999 or later.

"The NABE panel said tight money was likely to be a factor triggering the next recession, but the forecasters believe it will have little, if any, impact on the near-term outlook for the economy," the report stated.
Corporate profits will rise by 5.4 percent in 1997 and 3.6 percent in 1998, down from 7.0 percent in 1996, the group predicted.
The NABE raised its estimate for 1997 personal consumption expenditure growth to 3.3 percent from 2.3 percent in its February survey.
The forecast for 1997 industrial production growth was also boosted to a gain of 4.1 percent versus 3.1 percent previously.
The group saw the nation's merchandise trade deficit rising to $176 billion in 1997, up from February's estimate of $163.5 billion.
NABE boosted its forecast for 1997 export growth to 8.9 percent from 7.4 percent in the last report, but also increased its import growth estimate to 9.8 percent from 6.1 percent.
